title: Docs: explain batching SLO tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient), defaults, overrides, and troubleshooting
author: Wei Chen
release_notes: Public docs: new “Batching tiers” page; updates to API reference + SDK snippets; adds troubleshooting checklist and FAQ clarifying defaults/overrides.
body: Summary: This PR updates public documentation to introduce Redwood’s workload-aware batching defaults and the three customer-facing latency SLO tiers: fast, standard, and cost-efficient. It explains what each tier optimizes for, how Redwood selects a profile, how to choose a tier per route/use case, and how to override defaults (Hosted API request-level, route-level policy, Dedicated tenant/cluster override). It also adds a troubleshooting checklist focused on common post-migration issues (tail latency spikes, streaming jitter, throughput vs latency trade-offs, and override precedence confusion). Motivation: We’re rolling out tiered batching defaults in runtime 1.22; customers need a clear mental model and concrete examples so they can adopt defaults safely without accidentally degrading streaming UX or overpaying for throughput. Scope of docs changes: Adds a new conceptual page “Batching tiers (SLO defaults)” under Performance → Inference tuning; Updates API reference to document `batching_tier` parameter and the corresponding request header; Updates Python/TypeScript examples to show tier selection for chat (streaming) vs batch summarization; Adds “How defaults are chosen” section with high-level signals (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency) and an explicit note that Redwood does not do per-tenant real-time autotuning in this release; Adds FAQ: what happens if you don’t pick a tier (answer: standard by default, unless your route policy pins a tier); Adds Dedicated-specific notes on override precedence and where to view the effective tier in Console; Adds troubleshooting checklist and a short decision tree for latency vs cost issues. Key guidance included: Tier definitions (customer-facing): fast: prioritizes tail latency protection for interactive experiences and streaming; standard: balanced defaults for mixed workloads; cost-efficient: prioritizes throughput/$ per token with higher batching aggressiveness while maintaining published targets under typical loads. How to choose: fast for streaming chat endpoints, agent loops, user-facing autocomplete; standard for most APIs and mixed usage; cost-efficient for offline/batch jobs (summarization pipelines, embeddings at scale, rerank batches) and non-interactive endpoints. Overrides: Hosted API: per request via SDK parameter `batching_tier="fast"|"standard"|"cost_efficient"` (and header `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier` for raw REST callers); Route-level: policy config in Console/route configuration (documented as recommended for consistency and auditability); Dedicated: tenant/cluster override (documented precedence: customer override > route policy > platform default). Troubleshooting: If p99 increases after switching to fast: verify endpoint is actually set to fast (effective tier), check concurrent requests per route, ensure streaming is enabled for UI, and consider reducing concurrent tool calls or switching heavy routes to standard. If streaming feels “bursty”: confirm you’re using streaming responses end-to-end, and understand that tier selection affects queuing/batching but not token content; if UI jitter persists, fast tier is recommended and you may need to lower client-side chunk aggregation. If cost-efficient causes queueing: move interactive routes back to standard/fast, or apply cost-efficient only to batch routes; if you need both, split routes or create two policies pointing at the same model with different tiers. If overrides don’t seem to apply: check precedence (Dedicated override vs route policy), and confirm you’re not mixing request-level tier with a pinned route policy (docs now call out the behavior explicitly). Notes/limitations called out: Tiers are SLO defaults, not a guarantee for all workloads; workloads with extreme prompt lengths or highly bursty concurrency may still need route-level tuning or capacity adjustments; Tier selection does not change logging/retention or data handling; it only affects runtime scheduling/batching behavior; In overload, Redwood may apply backpressure and/or degrade gracefully; docs reference standard retry/timeout guidance rather than exposing internal modes. Rollout coordination: Copy aligns with Hosted API messaging and runtime rollout. Console screenshots are intentionally minimal in this PR (design is still landing), but we added textual pointers to where users can view ‘effective tier’ and ‘why this profile’. Related work: Runtime tiered defaults (runtime 1.22) and SDK parameter support are being shipped in parallel; this PR links to the example snippets that match the upcoming SDK releases. Testing: `docs:build` and `docs:linkcheck` passing; ran `npm test` for docs site; verified code samples compile (TypeScript) and run (Python) against current SDK APIs on main.
commits: docs(perf): add batching tiers overview + tier definitions
docs(api): document batching_tier parameter + header alias
docs(examples): add streaming chat fast tier example and batch summarization cost-efficient example
docs(troubleshooting): add tier selection/override precedence checklist
chore: fix broken links and normalize tier naming (cost-efficient vs cost_efficient)
review_thread: Elliot Price (review): Please avoid wording that implies a hard guarantee; recommend “targets” and “designed to meet” rather than “will meet.” Also add a short “what happens if I don’t pick a tier” FAQ.

Wei Chen (author): Updated tier language to “targets”/“designed to meet published latency targets” and added FAQ clarifying default is standard unless pinned by route policy. Pushed commit `docs(troubleshooting): add default behavior FAQ`.

Henry Cho (review): The parameter naming needs to match SDKs. Are we standardizing on `cost_efficient` in APIs but “cost-efficient” in UI copy? Please ensure the doc shows both and mentions accepted aliases (if any).

Wei Chen (author): Updated API reference to show `cost_efficient` value and the docs copy uses “cost-efficient” in prose. Added note: “SDKs accept `cost_efficient`; Console shows ‘cost-efficient’.” No aliases documented beyond header name.
Lauren Bishop (review): Dedicated section needs a clear precedence example. Customers keep mixing tenant override and per-request tier and then assuming per-request wins.
Wei Chen (author): Added a dedicated callout box: “Precedence: Dedicated override > route policy > request-level.” Included an example table with three scenarios and the effective tier.
Aisha Bello (review): Troubleshooting checklist should include what metrics to look at in Console (p95/p99, queue depth, batch size). Keep it high-level but actionable.
Wei Chen (author): Added “What to check” bullets: latency percentiles by route, queueing indicators, and batch size distribution. Avoided internal metric names; kept it Console-facing.

Sofia Ivanova (review): In the “How defaults are chosen” section, please explicitly state the selection considers streaming vs non-streaming and prompt length distribution (already in design), but don’t over-specify the scheduler knobs.
Wei Chen (author): Done—added a short paragraph on inputs/signals and removed the earlier mention of specific wait budgets/max batch tokens.
